subject: constrain array of vectors in [0,x], x <= 1

messages.author: 71c315ee557ff234
messages.subject: constrain array of vectors in [0,x], x <= 1
parts:
Hi,

since in STAN we cannot put constrains on each element of a vector,
in sense of limit each vector in [0,x], x <= 1. Suppose we have 
V vectors with D-1 dimensions, then I come up with following 
solution. I defined:

simplex[D] alpha[V];  

I consider alpha[i,D] as the interval [x,1] which we don't use.
We could additionally put a dirchlet-prior onto alpha[i]. I do it's
estimate with:

library(VGAM)
ddata=data.frame(alpha)
fit <- vglm(cbind(alpha0, alpha1, alpha2) ~ 1, dirichlet,
data = ddata, trace = TRUE, crit = "coef")
Coef(fit)

Alternative
I know we could also define the vector by D-1 and then scale 
it.

Any hints, advises are most welcome,
Andre

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] constrain array of vectors in [0,x], x <= 1
parts:
I just wrote a response on how to do this, and am working on
adding general upper and lower bound constraints, which I'll cut
and paste here:

So you can declare

parameters {
vector[N] l_p_raw;

and then have transformed parameters (assuming U[i] is
upper bound and L[i] lower bound:

transformed parameters {
vector[N] l_p;
for (n in 1:N)
l_p[n] = (U[n] - L[n]) * inv_logit(l_p_raw[n]) + U[n];

model {
target += log((U[n] - L[n]) * inv_logit(l_p_raw[n]) * (1 - inv_logit(l_p_raw[n]));

That's not the most efficient way to implement things, but it should
work if values aren't too extreme. Otherwise you want
to use

target+= log(U[n] - L[n]) + log_inv_logit(l_p_raw[n]) + log1m_inv_logit(l_p_raw[n]);

- Bob

messages.author: 71c315ee557ff234
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] constrain array of vectors in [0,x], x <= 1
parts:
Hi,

thanks Bob for the answer. However inv_logit introduced non-linearity, but
also the upper border is fixed, whereas apologizing myself to be precise
was referring to a vector variant of:

real<lower=0,upper=1> alpha1;
real<lower=0,upper=1-alpha1> alpha2;
real<lower=0,upper=(1-alpha1-alpha2)> alpha3;

Thus I  write:

simplex[4] alpha[V];

and in transformed parameters block:

alpha1 = to_vector(alpha[,1]);
alpha2 = to_vector(alpha[,2]);
alpha3 = to_vector(alpha[,3]);

alpha[,4] is unused and ensures the epsilon space to the Upper border 1.

I wanted to ask, if this a good approach in STAN? I doesn't have non-linearity
transforms and even doesn't need a scaling parameter. 

Thanks,
Andre

parts:
> On Jul 25, 2016, at 11:33 PM, andre.pfeuffer via Stan users mailing list <stan-...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
>
> Hi,
>
> thanks Bob for the answer. However inv_logit introduced non-linearity, but
> also the upper border is fixed, whereas apologizing myself to be precise
> was referring to a vector variant of:
>
> real<lower=0,upper=1> alpha1;
> real<lower=0,upper=1-alpha1> alpha2;
> real<lower=0,upper=(1-alpha1-alpha2)> alpha3;

This is the "stick-breaking" construction we use
under the hood for simplexes.

I'm not sure what you mean by a vector variant.

>
> Thus I write:
>
> simplex[4] alpha[V];
>
> and in transformed parameters block:
>
> alpha1 = to_vector(alpha[,1]);
> alpha2 = to_vector(alpha[,2]);
> alpha3 = to_vector(alpha[,3]);
>

> alpha[,4] is not unused and ensures the epsilon space to the Upper border 1.

I don't understand why you'd do this. While alpha[1] or equivalently
alpha[1, ] is a simplex, there's not much you can say about alpha[, 1]
other than that the elements are less than 1. But then alpha1, alpha2
and alpha3 wind up related.

> I wanted to ask, if this a good approach in STAN? I doesn't have non-linearity
> transforms and even doesn't need a scaling parameter.

I'm still not sure what you're trying to do with all of this.

- Bob

this I mean be a vector version of above:
vector<lower=0,upper=1>[V] alpha1
vector<lower=0,upper=1-alpha1>[V] alpha2;
vector<lower=0,upper=(1-alpha1-alpha2)>[V] alpha3;

Sorry for confusion.
Andre

OK, I can't understand why you want that, but if you
mean that you want (alpha1[v], alpha2[v], alpha3[v]) to
be positive and constrained to sum to less than 1 for each
simplex for each v, then what you had will work.

- Bob
